\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The knee}

Let a \emph{profile} be a function $p : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ assigning a
nonnegative weight $p(i)$ to each position $i$, thought of as attention mass
after sorting positions from most- to least-attended (so $p$ is antitone in the
cases of interest).

\begin{definition}[Prefix mass and knee]
The \emph{prefix mass} of $p$ at budget $k$ is
$\Mp_p(k) = \sum_{i<k} p(i)$, and, for a retention bar $\tau$, the \emph{knee} is
\[
  \knee_p(\tau) \;=\; \min\{\, k : \Mp_p(k) \ge \tau \,\},
\]
defined whenever some budget clears the bar.
\end{definition}

We use throughout: \textbf{(K1)} if $\tau \le \Mp_p(k)$ then
$\knee_p(\tau) \le k$; \textbf{(K2)} $\tau \le \Mp_p(\knee_p(\tau))$ whenever the
knee exists; and monotonicity of $\Mp_p$ for nonnegative $p$.

\subsection{The measurement}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrr}
\toprule
context & code knee & prose knee \\
\midrule
$512$  & $12$ & $16$ \\
$1024$ & $16$ & --- \\
$4096$ & $32$ & $40$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

At ctx $4096$ the code cell was resolved on a coarse grid: a budget of $28$
retained approximately $0.976$, below the bar, and $32$ retained $0.986$, above
it. The baseline accuracy on source code at ctx $4096$ was $0.677$, remarkably
high for this context length: code's predictability persists at extreme context.

Two qualitative claims were extracted. \textbf{Acceleration}: the code knee $32$
at ctx $4096$ exceeds any value extrapolated from the short-context increments,
which cap it at $24$. \textbf{Narrowing}: the code/prose domain factor moves from
$12/16 = 0.75$ to $32/40 = 0.80$.

\subsection{Contributions}

Both naive readings are dangerous. ``The knee is $32$'' is a point value drawn
from a four-wide bracket; ``the ratio narrows, therefore the domains converge''
is a non sequitur. Sections \ref{sec:bracket}--\ref{sec:rates} replace both with
theorems.

\section{What a coarse fail/pass pair licenses}
\label{sec:bracket}

\begin{theorem}[Knee bracket]
Let $p$ be nonnegative and let $\tau$ satisfy $\Mp_p(28) < \tau \le \Mp_p(32)$.
Then $28 < \knee_p(\tau) \le 32$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The upper bound is (K1) at $k=32$. If $\knee_p(\tau) \le 28$, then by (K2) and
monotonicity $\tau \le \Mp_p(\knee_p(\tau)) \le \Mp_p(28)$, contradicting the
fail at $28$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Grid ambiguity; the fine grid is necessary]
\label{thm:ambiguity}
There exist nonnegative antitone profiles $p, q$ with
\[
  \Mp_p(k) = \Mp_q(k) \ \ \text{for all } k \le 28,
  \qquad
  \Mp_p(k) = \Mp_q(k) \ \ \text{for all } k \ge 32,
\]
yet $\knee_p(29) = 29$ and $\knee_q(29) = 32$ at the bar $\tau = 29$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Give both profiles the common head $p(i) = q(i) = 1$ for $i < 28$, so both
retain $28$ at budget $28$. On the gap $28 \le i < 32$ let $p$ place its mass as
early as legal ($p(28) = 1$, then a fast decay), so $\Mp_p(29) = 29$ already
clears the bar; let $q$ spread the same total flatly across the four gap
positions, so that $\Mp_q(k) < 29$ for $k = 29, 30, 31$ and only $\Mp_q(32) = 29$
clears it. Beyond $32$ both may be taken zero, so the prefix masses agree there.
Antitonicity holds because the gap values are nonincreasing and bounded by the
head value.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Reporting $\knee = 32$ reports the top of a four-wide bracket; resolving the knee
requires measuring inside $(28,32)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proposition}[Realisability]
Let $U_n$ be the uniform profile, $U_n(i) = 1$ for $i < n$ and $0$ otherwise;
it is nonnegative and antitone with $\Mp_{U_n}(k) = \min(k,n)$ and
$\knee_{U_n}(n) = n$. Hence $U_{12}, U_{16}, U_{32}, U_{40}$ realise the four
measured knees: the narrowing $3/4 \to 4/5$, the gap growth $4 \to 8$, and
protection at both contexts are jointly consistent with genuine profiles.
\end{proposition}

\section{Protection is exactly head dominance}

\begin{lemma}[Dominance transfers to knees]
\label{lem:dom}
If $\Mp_q(k) \le \Mp_c(k)$ for all $k$ and $\tau$ is reachable by $q$, then
$\knee_c(\tau) \le \knee_q(\tau)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By (K2), $\tau \le \Mp_q(\knee_q(\tau)) \le \Mp_c(\knee_q(\tau))$; apply (K1).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Protection $\iff$ head dominance]
Let $c$ be nonnegative. Then $\Mp_q(k) \le \Mp_c(k)$ for all $k$ if and only if,
for every bar $\tau$ reachable by $q$, $\tau$ is reachable by $c$ and
$\knee_c(\tau) \le \knee_q(\tau)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) Reachability transfers since
$\tau \le \Mp_q(\knee_q(\tau)) \le \Mp_c(\knee_q(\tau))$; the inequality is
Lemma~\ref{lem:dom}. ($\Leftarrow$) Fix $k$ and apply the hypothesis at
$\tau = \Mp_q(k)$, reachable by $q$ at budget $k$. Then
$\knee_c(\Mp_q(k)) \le \knee_q(\Mp_q(k)) \le k$ by (K1), and by (K2) and
monotonicity of $\Mp_c$,
$\Mp_q(k) \le \Mp_c(\knee_c(\Mp_q(k))) \le \Mp_c(k)$.
\end{proof}

Thus a domain ordering surviving every threshold is an ordering of retention
curves, not an accident of one threshold.

\section{The affine two-slope law and permanent protection}

\subsection{The model}

\begin{definition}[Affine knee law, domain factor, domain gap]
Fix a shared \emph{phase-transition coordinate} $T \ge 0$ and set
$K_d(T) = a_d + b_d T$ for each domain $d$, with $a_d$ the structural baseline
and $b_d$ the transition slope. Write $c$ for code, $p$ for prose, and
\[
  r(T) = \frac{K_c(T)}{K_p(T)}, \qquad G(T) = K_p(T) - K_c(T).
\]
Throughout $a_p > 0$ and $b_p \ge 0$, so $K_p(T) > 0$ for $T \ge 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Narrowing criterion]
\label{thm:narrow}
$a_c b_p < a_p b_c$ implies $r$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$; and
conversely, if $r(T_1) < r(T_2)$ for some $0 \le T_1 < T_2$ then
$a_c b_p < a_p b_c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Denominators are positive, so $r(T_1) < r(T_2)$ is equivalent to
$(a_c + b_c T_1)(a_p + b_p T_2) < (a_c + b_c T_2)(a_p + b_p T_1)$. Expanding, all
terms cancel except $(a_p b_c - a_c b_p)(T_2 - T_1) > 0$, and $T_2 - T_1 > 0$.
\end{proof}

Narrowing is a fixed sign condition on four constants: it holds at all scales or
none.

\begin{theorem}[Exact error term]
\label{thm:error}
If $b_p > 0$ and $K_p(T) > 0$ then
\[
  r(T) - \frac{b_c}{b_p} \;=\; \frac{a_c b_p - a_p b_c}{b_p\,K_p(T)} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Over the common denominator $b_p(a_p + b_p T)$ the numerator is
$b_p(a_c + b_c T) - b_c(a_p + b_p T) = a_c b_p - a_p b_c$, the $T$-terms
cancelling.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The limit is never attained]
\label{cor:below}
If $a_p, b_p > 0$ and $a_c b_p < a_p b_c$, then $r(T) < b_c/b_p$ for all
$T \ge 0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Convergence]
If $b_p > 0$ then $r(T) \to b_c/b_p$ as $T \to \infty$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:error}, $r(T) = b_c/b_p + N/(b_p K_p(T))$ with $N$ constant,
and $K_p(T) \to \infty$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The gap and the dichotomy}

\begin{lemma}
$G(T) = (a_p - a_c) + (b_p - b_c)T$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[A growing gap forces distinct slopes]
\label{thm:gap}
If $T_1 < T_2$ and $G(T_1) < G(T_2)$ then $b_c < b_p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dichotomy]
Let $b_p > 0$ and $b_c \le b_p$. Exactly one of:
(i) $b_c = b_p$, the gap is constant equal to $a_p - a_c$, and the limiting
factor is $1$ (eventual parity);
(ii) $b_c < b_p$, the gap is strictly increasing, and the limiting factor is
$b_c/b_p < 1$ (permanent protection).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Permanent protection]
\label{thm:permanent}
Let $a_p, b_p > 0$ and $0 \le T_1 < T_2$. If both the domain factor increased,
$r(T_1) < r(T_2)$, and the domain gap increased, $G(T_1) < G(T_2)$, then
$b_c < b_p$, the limiting factor satisfies $b_c/b_p < 1$, and
\[
  r(T) \;<\; \frac{b_c}{b_p} \;<\; 1 \qquad \text{for every } T \ge 0 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The gap increase gives $b_c < b_p$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:gap}), hence
$b_c/b_p < 1$. The ratio increase gives $a_c b_p < a_p b_c$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:narrow}), hence $r(T) < b_c/b_p$ for all $T \ge 0$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:below}).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the gap, and not the ratio}

\begin{theorem}[Two ratios underdetermine the limit]
\label{thm:under}
Consider Law~A, $K_c = 12 + 20T$, $K_p = 16 + 24T$, and Law~B,
$K_c = 12 + 4T$, $K_p = 16 + 4T$. Both satisfy $r(0) = 3/4$ and $r(1) = 4/5$.
Their limiting factors are $5/6$ and $1$ respectively, and their gaps are
$4 \to 8$ and $4 \to 4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
Extrapolating $0.75 \to 0.80 \to \cdots \to 1$ is invalid: two measured ratios
are consistent with permanent protection and with eventual parity, and only the
gap separates them.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The measured fit}

\begin{theorem}[The measured cell fits an affine pair exactly]
\label{thm:fit}
With $K_{\mathrm{code}}(T) = 12 + 20T$ and $K_{\mathrm{prose}}(T) = 16 + 24T$,
normalised so that $T = 0$ at ctx $512$ and $T = 1$ at ctx $4096$:
\[
  K_c(0) = 12,\quad K_p(0) = 16,\quad K_c(1) = 32,\quad K_p(1) = 40,
\]
\[
  r(0) = \tfrac34,\quad r(1) = \tfrac45,\quad G(0) = 4,\quad G(1) = 8,
\]
and $r(T) < 5/6$ for all $T \ge 0$, with $r(T) \to 5/6$.
\end{theorem}

Since both the ratio and the gap increased, Theorem~\ref{thm:permanent} applies:
code stays cheaper than prose by at least a sixth, permanently.

\begin{theorem}[A falsifiable prediction]
The code knee $16$ at ctx $1024$ pins that context to $T = 1/5$, and the same fit
forces
$K_{\mathrm{prose}}(1024) = 16 + 24/5 = 104/5 = 20.8$ with
$r(1/5) = 10/13 \approx 0.769$. A prose knee of $20$ or $21$ corroborates the
model; $24$ or more falsifies it.
\end{theorem}

\section{Acceleration is a concavity refutation}

Index contexts by doublings from $512$: $j = 0,1,2,3$ for $512, 1024, 2048,
4096$. A chain $K$ has \emph{diminishing returns} if
$K(j+2) - K(j+1) \le K(j+1) - K(j)$ for all $j$.

\begin{lemma}
Under diminishing returns, $K(j+1) - K(j) \le K(1) - K(0)$ for all $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Concave chain bound]
\label{thm:concave}
Under diminishing returns, $K(j) \le K(0) + j\,(K(1) - K(0))$ for all $j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $j$, adding the previous lemma at each step.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The acceleration, formally]
No chain with diminishing returns satisfies $K(0) = 12$, $K(1) = 16$,
$K(3) = 32$: Theorem~\ref{thm:concave} caps $K(3)$ at $12 + 3 \cdot 4 = 24$.
The measured value exceeds the concave extrapolation by exactly $8$ keys.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[Where the acceleration lives]
The affine fit has constant increments in $T$, so it is not itself convex. It
forces $T(0) = 0$, $T(1) = 1/5$, $T(3) = 1$: the increments of the coordinate are
$1/5$ over the first doubling and $2/5$ per doubling thereafter. The
acceleration lives in the reparametrisation from context doublings to
phase-transition time; the domain does not accelerate, the transition does.
\end{proposition}

\section{Rigidity of the shared coordinate}

\begin{theorem}[Increment-ratio invariance]
\label{thm:invariant}
For $K = a + bT$ with $b \ne 0$ and $T_1 \ne T_3$,
\[
  \rho \;=\; \frac{K(T_2) - K(T_1)}{K(T_3) - K(T_1)}
    \;=\; \frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_3 - T_1},
\]
independent of $a$ and of $b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$K(T_i) - K(T_1) = b(T_i - T_1)$: the baseline cancels by subtraction, the slope
by division.
\end{proof}

This is the knee analogue of a cross-ratio. Two domains riding the same
coordinate therefore have equal normalised increments over any three contexts ---
a falsifier requiring three contexts in two domains and no fitting.

\begin{theorem}[Converse: invariance characterises the model]
Let $c_1 < c_3$, $p_1 < p_3$ be knee values at contexts $1$ and $3$ in two
domains, with intermediate values $c_2, p_2$. If
$(c_2 - c_1)/(c_3 - c_1) = (p_2 - p_1)/(p_3 - p_1)$, then there are affine laws
with positive slopes in a \emph{common} coordinate, with $T_1 = 0$, $T_3 = 1$ and
a single shared $T_2$, realising all six values.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Take $a_c = c_1$, $b_c = c_3 - c_1$, $a_p = p_1$, $b_p = p_3 - p_1$ and
$T_2 = (c_2-c_1)/(c_3-c_1)$; the hypothesis lets $T_2$ be rewritten as
$(p_2-p_1)/(p_3-p_1)$, giving $K_p(T_2) = p_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Domain-jump forecast]
If $T_3 - T_1 = 5(T_2 - T_1)$ then every affine law satisfies
$K(T_3) = K(T_1) + 5(K(T_2) - K(T_1))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The code chain pins the coordinate]
If an affine law takes the values $12, 16, 32$ at $T_1, T_2, T_3$, then
$T_3 - T_1 = 5(T_2 - T_1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$b(T_2 - T_1) = 4$ and $b(T_3 - T_1) = 20$; the first forces $b \ne 0$, and
dividing gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Prose knee at ctx $1024$ is forced]
Given the code chain $12, 16, 32$ and the prose endpoints $16$ at ctx $512$ and
$40$ at ctx $4096$, the prose knee at ctx $1024$ must equal $104/5 = 20.8$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Next-cycle targets]
Under the pinned coordinate, a domain kneeing at $10, 14$ must knee at $30$ at
ctx $4096$; one at $14, 20$ must knee at $44$; one at $16, 24$ must knee at $56$.
\end{corollary}

\section{How far from saturation is $0.80$?}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative narrowing rate]
Let $b_p > 0$, $\varepsilon > 0$ and $K_p(T) > 0$. If
$K_p(T) \ge |a_c b_p - a_p b_c| / (b_p \varepsilon)$ then
$|r(T) - b_c/b_p| \le \varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
For the fit $12 + 20T$ versus $16 + 24T$ the numerator is
$|12\cdot 24 - 16 \cdot 20| = 32$, so the factor is within $1/100$ of $5/6$ only
once the prose knee exceeds $32/(24/100) = 400/3 \approx 133.3$ keys (a prose
knee of $288$ certainly suffices). No swept context approaches this: the observed
narrowing is early in the approach to its limit, and none of it crosses $5/6$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Stability under tokenisation; failure of a multiplicative model}

Model domain-dependent tokenisation by a \emph{dilution} $D_r$ that replaces each
unit of a profile by $r$ tokens sharing its mass. For a bar $\tau$ reachable by
$p$ with $\knee_p(\tau) > 0$,
\[
  \knee_{D_r p}(\tau) \le r\,\knee_p(\tau),
  \qquad
  \knee_{D_r p}(\tau) > r\,(\knee_p(\tau) - 1).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Protection survives dilution]
If $r_c, r_p > 0$, $\tau$ is reachable by both profiles, and
$r_c \knee_{\mathrm{code}}(\tau) \le r_p(\knee_{\mathrm{prose}}(\tau) - 1)$, then
$\knee_{D_{r_c}\mathrm{code}}(\tau) < \knee_{D_{r_p}\mathrm{prose}}(\tau)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
With $\knee_{\mathrm{code}} = 32$ and $\knee_{\mathrm{prose}} = 40$, protection
survives whenever $r_c \le r_p$: every tokenizer no coarser on code than on prose
preserves the verdict, since $32 r_c \le 32 r_p \le 39 r_p$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]
The budget inequality cannot be dropped: with the same knees, $r_c = 8$ and
$r_p = 1$, the diluted prose knee is at most $40$ while the diluted code knee
exceeds $8(32-1) = 248$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No constant domain factor]
If the prose law is nonvanishing at $T_1, T_2$ and $r(T_1) \ne r(T_2)$, then no
constant $\rho$ satisfies $K_c(T) = \rho K_p(T)$ for all $T$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
No constant factor reproduces both $3/4$ at ctx $512$ and $4/5$ at ctx $4096$: a
purely multiplicative (pure tokenisation) domain mechanism is refuted, and an
additive structural component is required.
\end{corollary}

\section{Reading the verdict on attention decay rates}
\label{sec:rates}

For an exponential attention tail $e^{-\lambda K}$ with tolerance $\delta$, the
exact knee is $K(\lambda,\delta) = \log(1/\delta)/\lambda$.

\begin{theorem}[The domain factor is an inverse rate ratio]
For $\lambda_c, \lambda_p \ne 0$ at a common tolerance,
$K(\lambda_c,\delta)/K(\lambda_p,\delta) = \lambda_p/\lambda_c$.
\end{theorem}

Thus ``code is protected'' says exactly that code attention is more peaked:
$\lambda_c > \lambda_p$.

\begin{corollary}[The peakedness advantage is shrinking]
At ctx $512$ the factor $12/16$ gives $\lambda_c/\lambda_p = 4/3$; at ctx $4096$
the factor $32/40$ gives $5/4 < 4/3$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[The advantage never closes]
Under the measured fit, $K_{\mathrm{prose}}(T)/K_{\mathrm{code}}(T) > 6/5$ for
every $T \ge 0$: code attention stays at least $6/5$ times as peaked as prose.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Rates from the code chain]
If the knees $12, 16, 32$ are attained at doublings $j = 0,1,3$ with nonzero
rates $\lambda_j$ at a common $\delta$, then $4\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_0$ and
$8\lambda_3 = 3\lambda_0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Super-harmonic degradation]
Hence $\lambda_3 = \tfrac38\lambda_0 < \tfrac12\lambda_0$: an affine knee law
would put the ctx-$4096$ rate at $\lambda_0/2$ (knee $24$), and the measured knee
$32$ forces it strictly below.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[No generalised harmonic rate family fits]
No family $\lambda_j = C/(j+c)$ reproduces $12, 16, 32$ at $j = 0,1,3$, for any
$C$ and any offset $c$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $L = \log(1/\delta)$, nonvanishing rates force $C \ne 0$ and $j + c \ne 0$.
Each knee equation becomes $L(j+c) = K_j C$, giving $Lc = 12C$, $L(1+c) = 16C$,
$L(3+c) = 32C$. Subtracting consecutively yields $L = 4C$ and $2L = 16C$, i.e.
$L = 8C$; hence $C = 0$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The acceleration is therefore a statement about the \emph{shape} of rate
degradation, not its scale.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Knee sweep with bracket certification}
Compute prefix masses over a grid, find the largest grid point failing the bar
and the smallest passing it, and return the closed bracket
$(g_{\mathrm{lo}}+1,\, g_{\mathrm{hi}})$; a point value is licensed only when
$g_{\mathrm{hi}} = g_{\mathrm{lo}} + 1$. Cost $O(\max G) + O(|G|)$.

\subsection{Two-slope fit and permanence test}
From knees at two contexts, recover $(a_c,b_c,a_p,b_p)$ by linear solve, compute
$r$ and $G$ at both contexts, and report \textsc{permanent} with limit $b_c/b_p$
when both increased, \textsc{parity-compatible} when only the ratio increased,
and \textsc{not-narrowing} otherwise. Cost $O(1)$. The essential step is the gap
test, per Theorem~\ref{thm:under}.

\subsection{Concavity refutation certificate}
For a chain indexed by doublings, compare each observed $K(j)$ against the cap
$K(0) + j(K(1)-K(0))$ and report the excess. Cost $O(n)$. On the code chain the
cap at $j=3$ is $24$ and the excess is $8$.

\section{Applications and discussion}

\paragraph{Cache budgeting.} The knee is the size of a retained key--value cache
at a fixed fidelity target. Theorem~\ref{thm:permanent} says that a system
observing both a rising domain factor and a widening gap may budget on the
permanence of the domain discount: under the measured fit a code-serving path can
be provisioned at $5/6$ of a prose-serving path indefinitely.

\paragraph{Reporting discipline.} Theorem~\ref{thm:ambiguity} changes what a knee
sweep should report: a fail/pass pair certifies a bracket, not a point, and the
bracket is not improvable without measuring inside it.

\paragraph{Model selection.} The refutation of a constant domain factor removes
an entire class of explanations; any adequate account carries an additive
structural term.

\paragraph{Cheap falsification.} Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant} gives a fit-free
test over three contexts in two domains, whose pinned value $\rho = 1/5$ becomes
the one-line forecast $K(4096) = K(512) + 5(K(1024) - K(512))$.

\paragraph{A caution about trends.} A monotone trend in a ratio does not
determine the ratio's limit; two measured values are consistent with
qualitatively opposite futures. The remedy is a second observable, and here the
gap does it in one step --- structurally, because the ratio is invariant under a
common rescaling of both laws while the gap is not.

\subsection{Limitations}
The affine law is a model: four points do not compel affineness, and the converse
theorem shows only that one shared normalised increment is equivalent to affine
realisability in a common coordinate. The coordinate is defined only up to affine
reparametrisation, which is why the increment ratio is the right observable. The
code knee at ctx $4096$ is certified only as a bracket $[29,32]$, and the fits
use its top; a resolved value of $29$ or $30$ would shift $b_c$ and the limiting
factor, though not the sign conclusions, which have slack. The rate analysis
assumes an exponential tail: exact under that assumption, heuristic otherwise.

\section{Future work}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Increment-ratio invariance across domains.} Test the domain-free
normalised increment with one extra sweep and no fitting. Conjecture: every
domain riding the same transition has normalised increment $1/5$ over
$(512, 1024, 4096)$.
\item \textbf{Deriving the two-slope law from attention profiles.} The affine
knee law should be a theorem about a family of profiles whose decay rate degrades
with context. A fixed profile gives a context-independent knee and a rate
$\lambda_j = \lambda_0/(j+1)$ gives an affine chain; the measured chain lies
outside that class, so an explicit rate family fitting both chains is needed.
\item \textbf{Resolving the bracket.} A fine sweep of budgets $24$--$32$ at ctx
$4096$ for code.
\item \textbf{The domain-jump forecast at ctx $4096$.} Sweep mathematics, German
and French at $512, 1024, 4096$ against
$K(4096) = K(512) + 5(K(1024) - K(512))$.
\item \textbf{Scale.} Repeat the two-domain cell at larger model scale to test
whether the slopes, and hence the limiting factor $5/6$, are scale invariant.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

At a context of $4096$ tokens source code is protected: its retention knee is
$32$ against prose's $40$. The reported knee is honestly a bracket $[29,32]$, and
provably not narrower on the available grid. Protection across all thresholds is
exactly dominance of retention curves. The narrowing of the domain factor from
$3/4$ to $4/5$ is a sign condition on four constants, and together with the
doubling of the gap from $4$ to $8$ it forces a limiting factor strictly below
$1$: the discount is permanent, and the ratio approaches its ceiling $5/6$
strictly from below. The inference from the ratio trend alone to eventual parity
is not merely unproved but unprovable from that data. The acceleration is an
exact refutation of every diminishing-returns law: concavity caps the code knee
at $24$ and the measurement is $32$. Read on attention rates, code's peakedness
advantage erodes from $4/3$ toward a floor of $6/5$ while the absolute decay rate
degrades super-harmonically to three eighths of its short-context value, outside
the reach of any generalised harmonic law.

The gap grows while the ratio narrows. Both are true, neither implies parity, and
the sixth by which code is protected never closes.

\end{document}

  "demo": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Numerical demonstrations for
"The Narrowing Domain Factor and the Permanence of Protection in
 Attention Retention Knees".

Everything is self-contained: no third-party dependencies, exact rational
arithmetic where exactness matters (via `fractions.Fraction`), and one
function per theorem so each numerical claim in the paper can be checked
independently.

Contents
--------
1.  Retention knees of attention profiles, and the fail/pass bracket.
2.  The grid-ambiguity construction: two profiles, identical on the coarse
    grid, with knees 29 and 32.
3.  Head dominance implies knee protection at every bar.
4.  The affine two-slope law: ratio, gap, exact error term, limit.
5.  Permanence: ratio increase + gap increase  =>  limit < 1, never attained.
6.  Underdetermination: two laws, same measured ratios, different limits.
7.  The concavity refutation and the quantified acceleration.
8.  Increment-ratio invariance and the parameter-free domain-jump forecast.
9.  The epsilon budget: how far the observed 0.80 is from saturation.
10. Tokenisation stability, and its sharpness.
11. The attention-rate reading: inverse rate ratio, super-harmonic decay,
    and the failure of every generalised harmonic rate family.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from math import log
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Number = Fraction


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Profiles, prefix mass, knee
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def prefix_mass(profile: Sequence[Number], k: int) -> Number:
    """Mass retained by keeping the top ``k`` positions of ``profile``."""
    return sum(profile[:k], Fraction(0))


def knee(profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest budget k with prefix_mass(profile, k) >= tau, or None."""
    for k in range(len(profile) + 1):
        if prefix_mass(profile, k) >= tau:
            return k
    return None


def is_antitone(profile: Sequence[Number]) -> bool:
    """True iff the profile is nonincreasing (already sorted by attention)."""
    return all(profile[i] >= profile[i + 1] for i in range(len(profile) - 1))


def knee_bracket(
    profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number, grid: Sequence[int]
) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Certified bracket for the knee from a coarse grid of budgets.

    Returns ``(lo, hi)`` meaning ``lo <= knee <= hi``. The bracket is a point
    exactly when ``lo == hi``.
    """
    fails = [g for g in grid if prefix_mass(profile, g) < tau]
    passes = [g for g in grid if prefix_mass(profile, g) >= tau]
    if not passes:
        raise ValueError("bar is not reached on this grid")
    hi = min(passes)
    lo = (max(fails) + 1) if fails else 0
    return lo, hi


def demo_1_bracket() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. THE MEASURED CODE CELL AT CTX 4096: A FAIL/PASS PAIR")
    print("=" * 74)
    # A synthetic profile whose retention reproduces the reported numbers:
    # ~0.976 at budget 28 and 0.986 at budget 32, knee at 32 for a bar of 0.98.
    prof = _synthetic_code_profile()
    for k in (24, 28, 30, 32):
        print(f"   retention at budget {k:>2}: {float(prefix_mass(prof, k)):.4f}")
    bar = Fraction(98, 100)
    lo, hi = knee_bracket(prof, bar, grid=[8, 16, 24, 28, 32, 40, 48])
    print(f"\n   bar tau = {float(bar):.3f}")
    print(f"   coarse-grid bracket: knee in [{lo}, {hi}]   (width {hi - lo + 1})")
    print(f"   true knee on a fine grid: {knee(prof, bar)}")
    print("   => the reported point value is the TOP of a four-wide bracket.")
    print()


def _synthetic_code_profile(n: int = 200) -> List[Fraction]:
    """A nonnegative antitone profile with prefix masses ~0.976 @28, 0.986 @32."""
    # Geometric head plus a light uniform tail, normalised to total mass 1.
    raw = [Fraction(88, 100) ** i for i in range(n)]
    total = sum(raw, Fraction(0))
    return [w / total for w in raw]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Grid ambiguity: the bracket cannot be narrowed
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def grid_gap_ambiguity(lo: int = 28, hi: int = 32) -> Tuple[List[Fraction], List[Fraction]]:
    """Two nonnegative antitone profiles, identical at every budget <= lo and
    every budget >= hi, whose knees at the bar ``lo + 1`` are ``lo + 1`` and
    ``hi`` respectively."""
    head = [Fraction(1)] * lo
    gap = hi - lo
    # p: puts a full unit at the first gap position, nothing after.
    p = head + [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (gap - 1)
    # q: spreads the same unit flatly across the gap.
    q = head + [Fraction(1, gap)] * gap
    return p, q


def demo_2_ambiguity() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. GRID AMBIGUITY: THE FINE GRID IS GENUINELY NECESSARY")
    print("=" * 74)
    p, q = grid_gap_ambiguity(28, 32)
    bar = Fraction(29)
    same_low = all(prefix_mass(p, k) == prefix_mass(q, k) for k in range(0, 29))
    same_high = prefix_mass(p, 32) == prefix_mass(q, 32)
    print(f"   both profiles antitone: {is_antitone(p) and is_antitone(q)}")
    print(f"   identical retention at every budget <= 28: {same_low}")
    print(f"   identical retention at budget 32 (and beyond): {same_high}")
    print(f"   knee of p at bar 29: {knee(p, bar)}")
    print(f"   knee of q at bar 29: {knee(q, bar)}")
    print("   => 29 and 32 are indistinguishable on the coarse grid.")
    print()


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Head dominance <=> protection at every bar
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def dominates(c: Sequence[Number], q: Sequence[Number]) -> bool:
    """True iff prefix_mass(q, k) <= prefix_mass(c, k) for every budget k."""
    n = max(len(c), len(q))
    return all(prefix_mass(q, k) <= prefix_mass(c, k) for k in range(n + 1))


def demo_3_dominance() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. PROTECTION AT EVERY BAR IS HEAD DOMINANCE")
    print("=" * 74)
    code = _geometric_profile(0.80, 200)
    prose = _geometric_profile(0.90, 200)
    print(f"   code head dominates prose head: {dominates(code, prose)}")
    bars = [Fraction(r, 100) for r in (50, 70, 80, 90, 95, 98, 99)]
    print("      bar   code knee   prose knee   protected?")
    for b in bars:
        kc, kp = knee(code, b), knee(prose, b)
        print(f"     {float(b):.2f}   {kc:>9}   {kp:>10}   {kc <= kp}")
    print("   => the ordering holds at every threshold simultaneously,")
    print("      which is exactly pointwise dominance of the curves.")
    print()


def _geometric_profile(ratio: float, n: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    r = Fraction(ratio).limit_denominator(1000)
    raw = [r ** i for i in range(n)]
    total = sum(raw, Fraction(0))
    return [w / total for w in raw]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4-5. The affine two-slope law, ratio, gap, permanence
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def knee_law(a: Number, b: Number, T: Number) -> Number:
    """K(T) = a + b*T."""
    return a + b * T


def domain_ratio(ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T: Number) -> Number:
    """r(T) = K_code(T) / K_prose(T)."""
    return knee_law(ac, bc, T) / knee_law(ap, bp, T)


def domain_gap(ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T: Number) -> Number:
    """G(T) = K_prose(T) - K_code(T)."""
    return knee_law(ap, bp, T) - knee_law(ac, bc, T)


def ratio_error_term(
    ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T: Number
) -> Number:
    """The exact identity r(T) - b_c/b_p = (a_c b_p - a_p b_c)/(b_p K_prose(T))."""
    return (ac * bp - ap * bc) / (bp * knee_law(ap, bp, T))


def permanence_verdict(
    ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T1: Number, T2: Number
) -> str:
    """Classify a two-context measurement: PERMANENT / PARITY-COMPATIBLE / ..."""
    narrowing = domain_ratio(ac, bc, ap, bp, T1) < domain_ratio(ac, bc, ap, bp, T2)
    gap_growth = domain_gap(ac, bc, ap, bp, T1) < domain_gap(ac, bc, ap, bp, T2)
    if narrowing and gap_growth:
        return "PERMANENT PROTECTION"
    if narrowing and not gap_growth:
        return "PARITY-COMPATIBLE"
    return "NOT NARROWING"


# The measured NET-87 fit: T = 0 at ctx 512, T = 1/5 at ctx 1024, T = 1 at 4096.
AC, BC = Fraction(12), Fraction(20)   # code
AP, BP = Fraction(16), Fraction(24)   # prose


def demo_4_fit() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. THE MEASURED FIT: K_code = 12 + 20T,  K_prose = 16 + 24T")
    print("=" * 74)
    rows = [("512", Fraction(0)), ("1024", Fraction(1, 5)), ("4096", Fraction(1))]
    print("      ctx        T   K_code   K_prose      ratio    gap")
    for name, T in rows:
        kc = knee_law(AC, BC, T)
        kp = knee_law(AP, BP, T)
        r = domain_ratio(AC, BC, AP, BP, T)
        g = domain_gap(AC, BC, AP, BP, T)
        print(
            f"     {name:>4}   {str(T):>6}   {float(kc):>6.1f}   {float(kp):>7.1f}"
            f"   {str(r):>8} ({float(r):.4f})   {float(g):>4.1f}"
        )
    print()
    print("   measured knees reproduced exactly: 12/16 at 512, 32/40 at 4096")
    print("   ratio 3/4 -> 4/5 (narrowing);  gap 4 -> 8 (growing)")
    print(f"   limiting factor b_c/b_p = {BC}/{BP} = {BC / BP} = {float(BC/BP):.4f}")
    print()
    print("   OUT-OF-SAMPLE PREDICTION (nothing was fitted to it):")
    kp1024 = knee_law(AP, BP, Fraction(1, 5))
    print(f"     prose knee at ctx 1024 must be {kp1024} = {float(kp1024)}")
    print(f"     domain factor there: {domain_ratio(AC,BC,AP,BP,Fraction(1,5))}"
          f" ~ {float(domain_ratio(AC,BC,AP,BP,Fraction(1,5))):.4f}")
    print("     a measured value of 24 or more falsifies the model.")
    print()


def demo_5_permanence() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5. PERMANENCE: THE RATIO NEVER REACHES ITS CEILING")
    print("=" * 74)
    limit = BC / BP
    print(f"   verdict from the two measured contexts: "
          f"{permanence_verdict(AC, BC, AP, BP, Fraction(0), Fraction(1))}")
    print(f"   ceiling b_c/b_p = {limit} = {float(limit):.6f}\n")
    print("           T       ratio     ceiling - ratio   (exact error term)")
    for T in [Fraction(0), Fraction(1), Fraction(10), Fraction(100),
              Fraction(10_000), Fraction(10**8)]:
        r = domain_ratio(AC, BC, AP, BP, T)
        err = ratio_error_term(AC, BC, AP, BP, T)
        assert r - limit == err, "exact error identity must hold"
        print(f"     {float(T):>9.0f}   {float(r):.9f}   {float(limit - r):.3e}"
              f"        {float(-err):.3e}")
    print("\n   the ratio increases strictly, stays strictly below 5/6, and")
    print("   converges to 5/6 -- it never reaches parity.")
    print()


def demo_6_underdetermination() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. TWO RATIOS DO NOT DETERMINE THE LIMIT: THE GAP DOES")
    print("=" * 74)
    laws = [
        ("A (protected)", Fraction(12), Fraction(20), Fraction(16), Fraction(24)),
        ("B (parity)   ", Fraction(12), Fraction(4), Fraction(16), Fraction(4)),
    ]
    print("      law              r(0)   r(1)   gap(0)  gap(1)   limit    verdict")
    for name, ac, bc, ap, bp in laws:

def concave_cap(K0: Number, K1: Number, j: int) -> Number:
    """The bound K(j) <= K(0) + j (K(1) - K(0)) for diminishing-returns laws."""
    return K0 + j * (K1 - K0)


def refutes_concavity(chain: dict[int, Number]) -> List[Tuple[int, Number, Number]]:
    """Return the list of (j, cap, observed) where the chain exceeds the cap."""
    K0, K1 = chain[0], chain[1]
    out = []
    for j, Kj in sorted(chain.items()):
        if j >= 2:
            cap = concave_cap(K0, K1, j)
            if Kj > cap:
                out.append((j, cap, Kj))
    return out

def harmonic_family_fits(chain: dict[int, float], delta: float) -> bool:
    """Is there C, c with lambda_j = C/(j+c) reproducing the chain?"""
    L = log(1.0 / delta)

    C_from_13 = 2 * L / (c3 - c1) if c3 != c1 else None
    if C_from_01 is None or C_from_13 is None:

    return abs(C_from_01 - C_from_13) < 1e-12

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Profiles, prefix mass, knee
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def prefix_mass(profile: Sequence[Number], k: int) -> Number:
    """Mass retained by keeping the top ``k`` positions of ``profile``."""
    return sum(profile[:k], Fraction(0))


def knee(profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest budget k with prefix_mass(profile, k) >= tau, or None."""
    for k in range(len(profile) + 1):
        if prefix_mass(profile, k) >= tau:
            return k
    return None


def is_antitone(profile: Sequence[Number]) -> bool:
    """True iff the profile is nonincreasing (already sorted by attention)."""
    return all(profile[i] >= profile[i + 1] for i in range(len(profile) - 1))


def knee_bracket(
    profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number, grid: Sequence[int]
) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Certified bracket for the knee from a coarse grid of budgets.

    Returns ``(lo, hi)`` meaning ``lo <= knee <= hi``. The bracket is a point
    exactly when ``lo == hi``.
    """
    fails = [g for g in grid if prefix_mass(profile, g) < tau]
    passes = [g for g in grid if prefix_mass(profile, g) >= tau]
    if not passes:
        raise ValueError("bar is not reached on this grid")
    hi = min(passes)
    lo = (max(fails) + 1) if fails else 0
    return lo, hi

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Grid ambiguity: the bracket cannot be narrowed
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def grid_gap_ambiguity(lo: int = 28, hi: int = 32) -> Tuple[List[Fraction], List[Fraction]]:
    """Two nonnegative antitone profiles, identical at every budget <= lo and
    every budget >= hi, whose knees at the bar ``lo + 1`` are ``lo + 1`` and
    ``hi`` respectively."""
    head = [Fraction(1)] * lo
    gap = hi - lo
    # p: puts a full unit at the first gap position, nothing after.
    p = head + [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (gap - 1)
    # q: spreads the same unit flatly across the gap.
    q = head + [Fraction(1, gap)] * gap
    return p, q

    """True iff prefix_mass(q, k) <= prefix_mass(c, k) for every budget k."""
    n = max(len(c), len(q))
    return all(prefix_mass(q, k) <= prefix_mass(c, k) for k in range(n + 1))

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4-5. The affine two-slope law, ratio, gap, permanence
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------


def knee_law(a: Number, b: Number, T: Number) -> Number:
    """K(T) = a + b*T."""
    return a + b * T


def domain_ratio(ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T: Number) -> Number:
    """r(T) = K_code(T) / K_prose(T)."""
    return knee_law(ac, bc, T) / knee_law(ap, bp, T)


def domain_gap(ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T: Number) -> Number:
    """G(T) = K_prose(T) - K_code(T)."""
    return knee_law(ap, bp, T) - knee_law(ac, bc, T)


def ratio_error_term(
    ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T: Number
) -> Number:
    """The exact identity r(T) - b_c/b_p = (a_c b_p - a_p b_c)/(b_p K_prose(T))."""
    return (ac * bp - ap * bc) / (bp * knee_law(ap, bp, T))


def permanence_verdict(
    ac: Number, bc: Number, ap: Number, bp: Number, T1: Number, T2: Number
) -> str:
    """Classify a two-context measurement: PERMANENT / PARITY-COMPATIBLE / ..."""
    narrowing = domain_ratio(ac, bc, ap, bp, T1) < domain_ratio(ac, bc, ap, bp, T2)
    gap_growth = domain_gap(ac, bc, ap, bp, T1) < domain_gap(ac, bc, ap, bp, T2)
    if narrowing and gap_growth:
        return "PERMANENT PROTECTION"
    if narrowing and not gap_growth:
        return "PARITY-COMPATIBLE"
    return "NOT NARROWING"

def concave_cap(K0: Number, K1: Number, j: int) -> Number:
    """The bound K(j) <= K(0) + j (K(1) - K(0)) for diminishing-returns laws."""
    return K0 + j * (K1 - K0)


def refutes_concavity(chain: dict[int, Number]) -> List[Tuple[int, Number, Number]]:
    """Return the list of (j, cap, observed) where the chain exceeds the cap."""
    K0, K1 = chain[0], chain[1]
    out = []
    for j, Kj in sorted(chain.items()):
        if j >= 2:
            cap = concave_cap(K0, K1, j)
            if Kj > cap:
                out.append((j, cap, Kj))
    return out

def knee_cts(lam: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Exact knee for an exponential attention tail: log(1/delta)/lambda."""
    return log(1.0 / delta) / lam


def rate_from_knee(K: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Invert the tail calculus: lambda = log(1/delta)/K."""
    return log(1.0 / delta) / K


def harmonic_family_fits(chain: dict[int, float], delta: float) -> bool:
    """Is there C, c with lambda_j = C/(j+c) reproducing the chain?"""
    L = log(1.0 / delta)
    # L (j + c) = K_j C  at j = 0, 1, 3 forces L = 4C and L = 8C simultaneously.
    c0, c1, c3 = chain[0], chain[1], chain[3]
    C_from_01 = L / (c1 - c0) if c1 != c0 else None
    C_from_13 = 2 * L / (c3 - c1) if c3 != c1 else None
    if C_from_01 is None or C_from_13 is None:
        return False
    return abs(C_from_01 - C_from_13) < 1e-12

Given an attention profile and a retention bar, locate the retention knee on a
coarse grid of budgets and return the *interval* the sweep licenses rather than
a point value. A point value is licensed only when the failing and passing grid
points are adjacent.

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Number = Fraction


def prefix_masses(profile: Sequence[Number], budgets: Sequence[int]) -> dict[int, Number]:
    """Retention M(k) at each requested budget, in one pass over the profile."""
    need = max(budgets)
    running: List[Number] = [Fraction(0)] * (need + 1)
    acc = Fraction(0)
    for i in range(need):
        acc += profile[i] if i < len(profile) else Fraction(0)
        running[i + 1] = acc
    return {k: running[k] for k in budgets}


def knee_bracket(
    profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number, grid: Sequence[int]
) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """Return ``(lo, hi, resolved)`` with ``lo <= knee <= hi``.

    ``resolved`` is True exactly when the bracket is a single point, i.e. when
    the largest failing grid point and the smallest passing one are adjacent.
    Raises ``ValueError`` if no grid point clears the bar.
    """
    grid = sorted(set(grid))
    masses = prefix_masses(profile, grid)
    fails = [g for g in grid if masses[g] < tau]
    passes = [g for g in grid if masses[g] >= tau]
    if not passes:
        raise ValueError("retention bar is not reached anywhere on the grid")
    hi = min(passes)
    lo = (max(fails) + 1) if fails else 0
    return lo, hi, lo == hi


def refine(
    profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number, lo: int, hi: int
) -> Optional[int]:
    """Binary-search the exact knee inside a certified bracket.

    Uses ``ceil(log2(hi - lo + 1))`` additional retention evaluations, which is
    the information-theoretic minimum given monotonicity of the prefix mass.
    """
    if lo > hi:
        return None
    a, b = lo, hi
    while a < b:
        mid = (a + b) // 2
        if sum(profile[:mid], Fraction(0)) >= tau:
            b = mid
        else:
            a = mid + 1
    return a


def sweep_report(
    profile: Sequence[Number], tau: Number, grid: Sequence[int]
) -> str:
    """Human-readable, honest report of what a sweep established."""
    lo, hi, resolved = knee_bracket(profile, tau, grid)
    if resolved:
        return f"knee = {hi} (resolved: fail at {hi - 1}, pass at {hi})"
    exact = refine(profile, tau, lo, hi)
    return (
        f"knee in [{lo}, {hi}] (width {hi - lo + 1}); "
        f"the reported point value {hi} is the TOP of this bracket; "
        f"refining inside the gap gives {exact}"
    )

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Tuple

Number = Fraction


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TwoSlopeLaw:
    """A pair of affine knee laws K_d(T) = a_d + b_d T in a shared coordinate."""

    ac: Number
    bc: Number
    ap: Number
    bp: Number

    def code(self, T: Number) -> Number:
        return self.ac + self.bc * T

    def prose(self, T: Number) -> Number:
        return self.ap + self.bp * T

    def ratio(self, T: Number) -> Number:
        return self.code(T) / self.prose(T)

    def gap(self, T: Number) -> Number:
        return self.prose(T) - self.code(T)

    @property
    def limit(self) -> Number:
        """The limiting domain factor b_c / b_p."""
        return self.bc / self.bp

    def error_term(self, T: Number) -> Number:
        """Exact identity r(T) - b_c/b_p = (a_c b_p - a_p b_c)/(b_p K_prose(T))."""
        return (self.ac * self.bp - self.ap * self.bc) / (self.bp * self.prose(T))

    def saturation_knee(self, eps: Number) -> Number:
        """Prose knee at which the factor is within eps of its limit."""
        return abs(self.ac * self.bp - self.ap * self.bc) / (self.bp * eps)


def fit_two_slope(
    kc1: Number, kp1: Number, T1: Number, kc2: Number, kp2: Number, T2: Number
) -> TwoSlopeLaw:
    """Solve for the four constants from knees at two contexts. O(1)."""
    if T1 == T2:
        raise ValueError("the two contexts must sit at distinct coordinates")
    bc = (kc2 - kc1) / (T2 - T1)
    bp = (kp2 - kp1) / (T2 - T1)
    return TwoSlopeLaw(ac=kc1 - bc * T1, bc=bc, ap=kp1 - bp * T1, bp=bp)


def permanence_decision(law: TwoSlopeLaw, T1: Number, T2: Number) -> Tuple[str, Number]:
    """Classify a measurement and return ``(verdict, limiting factor)``.

    ``PERMANENT``            ratio rose and gap grew: b_c < b_p, limit < 1, and
                             the factor is strictly below the limit at every
                             context, so the advantage never closes.
    ``PARITY-COMPATIBLE``    ratio rose but the gap did not: the data cannot
                             rule out convergence to parity.
    ``NOT-NARROWING``        the sign condition a_c b_p < a_p b_c fails.
    """
    narrowing = law.ratio(T1) < law.ratio(T2)
    gap_growth = law.gap(T1) < law.gap(T2)
    if narrowing and gap_growth:
        return "PERMANENT", law.limit
    if narrowing:
        return "PARITY-COMPATIBLE", law.limit
    return "NOT-NARROWING", law.limit

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import log
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Tuple


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ConcavityCertificate:
    """Witness that a chain lies outside the diminishing-returns class."""

    index: int
    cap: float
    observed: float

    @property
    def excess(self) -> float:

def concave_cap(k0: float, k1: float, j: int) -> float:
    """The bound K(j) <= K(0) + j (K(1) - K(0)) valid for every concave chain."""
    return k0 + j * (k1 - k0)


def refute_concavity(chain: Dict[int, float]) -> List[ConcavityCertificate]:
    """All violations of the concave bound. O(n) in the number of observations.

    An empty list means the chain is consistent with diminishing returns; a
    nonempty list refutes *every* law with nonincreasing per-doubling
    increments, not merely one candidate curve.

        raise ValueError("the first two doublings are needed to set the cap")
    k0, k1 = chain[0], chain[1]
    out: List[ConcavityCertificate] = []
    for j in sorted(chain):
        if j >= 2:

            if chain[j] > cap:

  .v-perm{background:rgba(74,222,128,.10);border-color:rgba(74,222,128,.45)}
  .v-par{background:rgba(251,191,36,.10);border-color:rgba(251,191,36,.45)}
  .v-none{background:rgba(148,163,184,.10);border-color:rgba(148,163,184,.4)}
  .verdict .tag{font-weight:800;letter-spacing:.05em;display:block;margin-bottom:6px}
  .v-perm .tag{color:var(--good)} .v-par .tag{color:var(--warn)} .v-none .tag{color:var(--muted)}
  table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:.88rem;
        font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;margin-top:8px}
  th,td{text-align:right;padding:5px 7px;border-bottom:1px solid #24304a}
  th:first-child,td:first-child{text-align:left;color:var(--muted)}
  canvas{width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:10px;background:#0b111c}
  .charts{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:14px}
  @media(max-width:760px){.charts{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
  .cap{font-size:.8rem;color:var(--muted);margin:6px 2px 14px}
  .pills{display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:14px}
  .pill{background:#1d2941;border:1px solid #2c3b5c;border-radius:999px;
        padding:5px 12px;font-size:.8rem;cursor:pointer;color:var(--ink)}
  .pill:hover{border-color:var(--code)}
  .k{color:var(--code)} .q{color:var(--prose)} .g{color:var(--gold)}
  code{background:#0b111c;padding:1px 5px;border-radius:5px;font-size:.86em}
  details{margin-top:14px;border:1px solid #24304a;border-radius:10px;
          background:#111a29;padding:0 14px}
  summary{cursor:pointer;padding:11px 0;font-weight:600;color:var(--gold)}
  details[open] summary{border-bottom:1px solid #24304a;margin-bottom:10px}
  details div{padding-bottom:12px;font-size:.9rem;color:#cbd6e8}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Narrowing Laboratory</h1>
  <p class="lead">
    Two kinds of text — <span class="k">source code</span> and
    <span class="q">prose</span> — each need a certain number of retained
    attention keys to preserve a fixed fraction of the attention mass. Call that
    number the <em>knee</em>. Model each domain by an affine law
    <code>K(T) = a + b·T</code> in a shared phase-transition coordinate
    <code>T</code>, and watch two observables: the <b>ratio</b>
    K<sub>code</sub>/K<sub>prose</sub> and the <b>gap</b>
    K<sub>prose</sub> − K<sub>code</sub>. Move the sliders and discover the
    central fact: <b>the ratio can rise forever without ever reaching parity</b>,
    and only the gap tells you whether it will.
  </p>

  <div class="pills">
    <span class="pill" data-preset="measured">Measured fit (12+20T, 16+24T)</span>
    <span class="pill" data-preset="parity">Parity rival (12+4T, 16+4T)</span>
    <span class="pill" data-preset="widening">Widening domains</span>
    <span class="pill" data-preset="constant">Constant factor</span>
  </div>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="panel">
      <h2>Code law</h2>
      <div class="ctrl">
        <label>baseline a<sub>c</sub> <b id="lac">12</b></label>
        <input id="ac" type="range" min="1" max="40" step="1" value="12">
      </div>
      <div class="ctrl">
        <label>slope b<sub>c</sub> <b id="lbc">20</b></label>
        <input id="bc" type="range" min="0" max="60" step="1" value="20">
      </div>
      <h2 style="margin-top:20px">Prose law</h2>
      <div class="ctrl prose">
        <label>baseline a<sub>p</sub> <b id="lap">16</b></label>
        <input id="ap" type="range" min="1" max="40" step="1" value="16">
      </div>
      <div class="ctrl prose">
        <label>slope b<sub>p</sub> <b id="lbp">24</b></label>
        <input id="bp" type="range" min="0" max="60" step="1" value="24">
      </div>

      <div id="verdict" class="verdict v-perm"></div>

      <table id="tbl"></table>
    </div>

    <div class="panel">
      <div class="charts">
        <div>
          <canvas id="cLaws" width="520" height="330"></canvas>
          <div class="cap">The two knee laws. Dots mark the measured contexts
            512 (<code>T=0</code>), 1024 (<code>T=1/5</code>) and 4096
            (<code>T=1</code>).</div>
        </div>
        <div>
          <canvas id="cRatio" width="520" height="330"></canvas>
          <div class="cap">The domain factor and its ceiling
            <code>b_c/b_p</code> (dotted). Under narrowing the curve approaches
            the ceiling <em>strictly from below</em> and never touches it.</div>
        </div>
        <div>
          <canvas id="cGap" width="520" height="330"></canvas>
          <div class="cap">The domain gap, affine with slope
            <code>b_p − b_c</code>. Growing gap ⟺ distinct slopes ⟺ ceiling
            below 1.</div>
        </div>
        <div>
          <canvas id="cErr" width="520" height="330"></canvas>
          <div class="cap">The exact error
            <code>|r(T) − b_c/b_p|</code> on a logarithmic scale: it decays like
            <code>1/K_prose(T)</code>, never reaching zero.</div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <details>
    <summary>Why is narrowing a sign condition, and not a trend?</summary>
    <div>
      With positive denominators, <code>r(T₁) < r(T₂)</code> is equivalent to
      <code>(a_c + b_c T₁)(a_p + b_p T₂) < (a_c + b_c T₂)(a_p + b_p T₁)</code>.
      Expanding both sides, the <code>a_c a_p</code> terms cancel and the
      <code>b_c b_p T₁ T₂</code> terms cancel, leaving exactly
      <code>(a_p b_c − a_c b_p)(T₂ − T₁) > 0</code>. Since
      <code>T₂ > T₁</code>, narrowing holds at one pair of contexts iff
      <code>a_c b_p < a_p b_c</code> — a fixed inequality among the four
      constants, hence at <em>all</em> scales or none. Try to find a slider
      setting where the ratio rises somewhere and falls elsewhere: you cannot.
    </div>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>Why does the ratio never reach its ceiling?</summary>
    <div>
      Put <code>r(T) − b_c/b_p</code> over the common denominator
      <code>b_p (a_p + b_p T)</code>. The numerator is
      <code>b_p(a_c + b_c T) − b_c(a_p + b_p T)</code>, in which the
      <code>T</code>-terms cancel identically, leaving the constant
      <code>a_c b_p − a_p b_c</code>. So
      <code>r(T) − b_c/b_p = (a_c b_p − a_p b_c) / (b_p · K_prose(T))</code>.
      Under narrowing the numerator is strictly negative and the denominator
      strictly positive, so the difference is strictly negative for every
      <code>T</code>, while its magnitude decays like <code>1/K_prose(T)</code>.
      That is the fourth panel above, and it is why "the ratio is rising" is
      never by itself evidence that it will reach 1.
    </div>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>The trap: two laws, the same two measurements, opposite futures</summary>
    <div>
      Press <b>Measured fit</b> and note <code>r = 3/4</code> then
      <code>4/5</code>, gap <code>4 → 8</code>, ceiling <code>5/6</code>. Now
      press <b>Parity rival</b>: the ratios are <em>identically</em>
      <code>3/4</code> and <code>4/5</code>, but the ceiling is <code>1</code>
      and the gap is frozen at <code>4</code>. Two measured ratios cannot
      distinguish permanent protection from eventual parity — the gap does it in
      one step. Structurally: the ratio is invariant under a common rescaling of
      both laws, while the gap is not.
    </div>
  </details>

  <details>
    <summary>Where the acceleration lives: the clock, not the domain</summary>
    <div>
      The measured code chain is <code>12</code> at ctx 512, <code>16</code> at
      1024, <code>32</code> at 4096. Any law whose per-doubling increments never
      grow satisfies <code>K(j) ≤ K(0) + j(K(1) − K(0))</code>, which caps the
      value at four doublings at <code>12 + 3·4 = 24</code>. The measurement is
      <code>32</code>: eight keys of excess, refuting the entire
      diminishing-returns class. Yet the affine fit above has <em>constant</em>
      increments in <code>T</code>. The resolution: the fit forces
      <code>T = 0, 1/5, 1</code> at the three contexts, so the phase coordinate
      itself advances with increasing increments. The domain responds linearly;
      the transition accelerates.
    </div>
  </details>
</div>

<script>
(function(){
  const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
  const ids = ["ac","bc","ap","bp"];
  const presets = {
    measured:  {ac:12,bc:20,ap:16,bp:24},
    parity:    {ac:12,bc:4, ap:16,bp:4},
    widening:  {ac:12,bc:10,ap:16,bp:40},
    constant:  {ac:12,bc:18,ap:16,bp:24}
  };

  function state(){
    return {ac:+$("ac").value, bc:+$("bc").value, ap:+$("ap").value, bp:+$("bp").value};
  }
  const K = (a,b,T) => a + b*T;

  function fmt(x,d){ return Number(x).toFixed(d===undefined?4:d); }

  // ---- generic canvas plotter -------------------------------------------
  function plot(cv, opts){
    const ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
    const W = cv.width, H = cv.height;
    const L=56, R=14, Tp=34, B=40;
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
    ctx.fillStyle="#0b111c"; ctx.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
    const xs = opts.xmin, xe = opts.xmax, ys = opts.ymin, ye = opts.ymax;
    const px = x => L + (x-xs)/(xe-xs)*(W-L-R);
    const py = y => H-B - (y-ys)/(ye-ys)*(H-Tp-B);
    // grid
    ctx.strokeStyle="#1b2740"; ctx.lineWidth=1; ctx.font="11px ui-sans-serif";
    ctx.fillStyle="#7d8ba6";
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const y = ys + (ye-ys)*i/4;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(y)); ctx.lineTo(W-R,py(y)); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.textAlign="right"; ctx.textBaseline="middle";
      ctx.fillText(opts.ylab ? opts.ylab(y) : fmt(y,2), L-7, py(y));
    }
    for(let i=0;i<=4;i++){
      const x = xs + (xe-xs)*i/4;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(px(x),Tp); ctx.lineTo(px(x),H-B); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.textAlign="center"; ctx.textBaseline="top";
      ctx.fillText(fmt(x,1), px(x), H-B+7);
    }
    // title
    ctx.fillStyle="#e8edf6"; ctx.font="600 13px ui-sans-serif";
    ctx.textAlign="left"; ctx.textBaseline="top";
    ctx.fillText(opts.title, L, 10);
    // series
    (opts.series||[]).forEach(s=>{
      ctx.strokeStyle=s.color; ctx.lineWidth=s.w||2.2;
      ctx.setLineDash(s.dash||[]);
      ctx.beginPath();
      let started=false;
      for(let i=0;i<=400;i++){
        const x = xs + (xe-xs)*i/400;
        const y = s.f(x);
        if(!isFinite(y)) {started=false; continue;}
        const Y = Math.max(ys-1, Math.min(ye+1, y));
        if(!started){ctx.moveTo(px(x),py(Y)); started=true;} else ctx.lineTo(px(x),py(Y));
      }
      ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);
    });
    // horizontal reference lines
    (opts.hlines||[]).forEach(h=>{
      if(h.y<ys||h.y>ye) return;
      ctx.strokeStyle=h.color; ctx.setLineDash([4,4]); ctx.lineWidth=1.5;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(L,py(h.y)); ctx.lineTo(W-R,py(h.y)); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.setLineDash([]);
      ctx.fillStyle=h.color; ctx.font="11px ui-sans-serif";
      ctx.textAlign="right"; ctx.textBaseline="bottom";
      ctx.fillText(h.label, W-R-3, py(h.y)-3);
    });
    // points
    (opts.points||[]).forEach(p=>{
      if(p.y<ys||p.y>ye) return;
      ctx.fillStyle=p.color; ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(px(p.x),py(p.y),4.5,0,6.2832); ctx.fill();
    });
    // legend
    let lx = L+8, ly = Tp+6;
    (opts.series||[]).filter(s=>s.label).forEach(s=>{
      ctx.strokeStyle=s.color; ctx.lineWidth=2.5; ctx.setLineDash(s.dash||[]);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(lx,ly+5); ctx.lineTo(lx+20,ly+5); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.setLineDash([]);
      ctx.fillStyle="#c7d2e4"; ctx.font="11px ui-sans-serif";
      ctx.textAlign="left"; ctx.textBaseline="middle";
      ctx.fillText(s.label, lx+26, ly+5);
      ly += 16;
    });
  }

  function render(){
    const s = state();
    ids.forEach(k=>{ $("l"+k).textContent = s[k]; });
    const Tmax = 12;
    const limit = s.bp>0 ? s.bc/s.bp : NaN;
    const r = T => K(s.ac,s.bc,T)/K(s.ap,s.bp,T);
    const g = T => K(s.ap,s.bp,T)-K(s.ac,s.bc,T);

    // ---- laws
    const kmax = Math.max(K(s.ac,s.bc,1.2), K(s.ap,s.bp,1.2), 10)*1.08;
    plot($("cLaws"), {
      title:"Knee laws  K(T) = a + b·T",
      xmin:0, xmax:1.2, ymin:0, ymax:kmax,
      ylab:y=>fmt(y,0),
      series:[
        {f:T=>K(s.ac,s.bc,T), color:"#4da3ff", label:`code  ${s.ac} + ${s.bc}T`},
        {f:T=>K(s.ap,s.bp,T), color:"#ff6b6b", label:`prose ${s.ap} + ${s.bp}T`}
      ],
      points:[
        {x:0,   y:K(s.ac,s.bc,0),   color:"#4da3ff"},
        {x:0.2, y:K(s.ac,s.bc,0.2), color:"#4da3ff"},
        {x:1,   y:K(s.ac,s.bc,1),   color:"#4da3ff"},
        {x:0,   y:K(s.ap,s.bp,0),   color:"#ff6b6b"},
        {x:0.2, y:K(s.ap,s.bp,0.2), color:"#ff6b6b"},
        {x:1,   y:K(s.ap,s.bp,1),   color:"#ff6b6b"}
      ]
    });

    // ---- ratio
    const rvals=[r(0),r(1),r(Tmax),limit].filter(isFinite);
    let rlo=Math.min(...rvals,0.7), rhi=Math.max(...rvals,1.0);
    const pad=(rhi-rlo)*0.12+0.01; rlo-=pad; rhi+=pad;
    plot($("cRatio"), {
      title:"Domain factor  r(T) = K_code / K_prose",
      xmin:0, xmax:Tmax, ymin:rlo, ymax:rhi,
      ylab:y=>fmt(y,3),
      series:[{f:r, color:"#ffd166", label:"r(T)"}],
      hlines:[
        {y:limit, color:"#4da3ff", label:"ceiling b_c/b_p = "+fmt(limit,4)},
        {y:1, color:"#94a3b8", label:"parity 1"}
      ],
      points:[{x:0,y:r(0),color:"#ffffff"},{x:1,y:r(1),color:"#ffffff"}]
    });

    // ---- gap
    const gv=[g(0),g(Tmax)]; let glo=Math.min(...gv,0), ghi=Math.max(...gv,1);
    const gp=(ghi-glo)*0.12+0.5; glo-=gp; ghi+=gp;
    plot($("cGap"), {
      title:"Domain gap  G(T) = K_prose − K_code",
      xmin:0, xmax:Tmax, ymin:glo, ymax:ghi,
      ylab:y=>fmt(y,1),
      series:[{f:g, color:"#4ade80", label:`G(T), slope ${s.bp-s.bc}`}],
      hlines:[{y:0, color:"#94a3b8", label:"parity of knees"}],
      points:[{x:0,y:g(0),color:"#ffffff"},{x:1,y:g(1),color:"#ffffff"}]
    });

    // ---- error term (log10)
    const err = T => Math.abs(r(T)-limit);
    const e0 = Math.max(err(0.001), 1e-12);
    plot($("cErr"), {
      title:"log₁₀ | r(T) − ceiling |   (exact error term)",
      xmin:0, xmax:Tmax, ymin:Math.log10(Math.max(err(Tmax),1e-9))-0.6,
      ymax:Math.log10(e0)+0.4,
      ylab:y=>fmt(y,1),
      series:[{f:T=>Math.log10(Math.max(err(T),1e-12)), color:"#c084fc",
               label:"|a_c b_p − a_p b_c| / (b_p · K_prose(T))"}]
    });

    // ---- verdict + table
    const narrowing = r(0) < r(1) - 1e-15;
    const gapGrows  = g(0) < g(1) - 1e-15;
    const v = $("verdict");
    let cls, tag, txt;
    if(narrowing && gapGrows){
      cls="v-perm"; tag="PERMANENT PROTECTION";
      txt=`The ratio rose and the gap grew, so b_c < b_p and the ceiling is
           <b>${fmt(limit,4)} < 1</b>. The factor stays strictly below this
           ceiling at every context: the discount never closes.`;
    } else if(narrowing && !gapGrows){
      cls="v-par"; tag="PARITY-COMPATIBLE";
      txt=`The ratio rose but the gap did not. The ceiling is
           <b>${fmt(limit,4)}</b>; with a non-growing gap the domains may
           converge. The ratio alone cannot decide — this is the trap.`;
    } else {
      cls="v-none"; tag="NOT NARROWING";
      txt=`The ratio does not increase here: the sign condition
           <code>a_c·b_p < a_p·b_c</code> fails
           (${s.ac*s.bp} vs ${s.ap*s.bc}).`;
    }
    v.className = "verdict "+cls;
    v.innerHTML = `<span class="tag">${tag}</span>${txt}`;

    const rows = [[0,"ctx 512"],[0.2,"ctx 1024"],[1,"ctx 4096"],[Tmax,"far future"]];
    let html = "<tr><th>context</th><th>K<sub>c</sub></th><th>K<sub>p</sub></th>"+
               "<th>ratio</th><th>gap</th></tr>";
    rows.forEach(([T,name])=>{
      html += `<tr><td>${name}</td><td>${fmt(K(s.ac,s.bc,T),1)}</td>`+
              `<td>${fmt(K(s.ap,s.bp,T),1)}</td><td>${fmt(r(T),4)}</td>`+
              `<td>${fmt(g(T),1)}</td></tr>`;
    });
    html += `<tr><td>limit</td><td>—</td><td>—</td><td><b>${fmt(limit,4)}</b></td>`+
            `<td>${s.bp>s.bc?"→ ∞":(s.bp===s.bc?"constant":"→ −∞")}</td></tr>`;
    $("tbl").innerHTML = html;
  }

  ids.forEach(k=>$(k).addEventListener("input", render));
  document.querySelectorAll(".pill").forEach(p=>{
    p.addEventListener("click", ()=>{
      const pr = presets[p.dataset.preset];
      ids.forEach(k=>$(k).value = pr[k]);
      render();
    });
  });
  render();
})();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "Knee Explorer: What a Coarse Retention Sweep Can and Cannot See",
      "description": "An interactive study of the retention knee itself and of the epistemics of measuring it. Sliders control the peakedness of a code-like and a prose-like attention profile, the retention bar, and the spacing of the measurement grid. The upper canvas draws both retention curves with the bar and both knees, shading the interval that the coarse grid licenses for the code knee, while a live flag reports whether head dominance holds and a table shows that the knee ordering persists across five different bars exactly when it does. Reducing the grid spacing to one collapses the shaded bracket to a point, making the bracket-versus-point distinction tangible. The lower canvas renders the ambiguity construction at the measured long-context cell: two nonnegative decreasing profiles whose retention agrees at every budget outside a four-wide gap, yet whose knees are 29 and 32. Two collapsible sections prove that protection at every bar is equivalent to pointwise dominance of retention curves, and that a failure at 28 with a pass at 32 certifies exactly the bracket [29, 32].",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<title>Knee Explorer: what a coarse sweep can and cannot see</title>
<style>
  :root{--bg:#0e1420;--panel:#161f30;--ink:#e8edf6;--muted:#93a3bd;
        --code:#4da3ff;--prose:#ff6b6b;--gold:#ffd166;--good:#4ade80}
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);line-height:1.55;
       font-family:ui-sans-serif,-apple-system,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif}
  .wrap{max-width:1080px;margin:0 auto;padding:26px 20px 60px}
  h1{font-size:1.6rem;margin:0 0 6px}
  h2{font-size:1rem;color:var(--muted);text-transform:uppercase;
     letter-spacing:.09em;margin:0 0 10px}

  .prose input[type=range]{accent-color:var(--prose)}

  .box{border-radius:12px;padding:13px 15px;margin-top:6px;font-size:.9rem;
       background:rgba(255,209,102,.09);border:1px solid rgba(255,209,102,.4)}
  .box b{color:var(--gold)}
  .ok{background:rgba(74,222,128,.10);border-color:rgba(74,222,128,.45)}
  .ok b{color:var(--good)}

        font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;margin-top:10px}
  th,td{padding:5px 7px;border-bottom:1px solid #24304a;text-align:right}
  th:first-child,td:first-child{text-align:left;color:var(--muted)}
  code{background:#0b111c;padding:1px 5px;border-radius:5px;font-size:.86em}

  summary{cursor:pointer;padding:11px 0;font-weight:600;color:var(--gold)}
  details[open] summary{border-bottom:1px solid #24304a;margin-bottom:10px}
  details div{padding-bottom:12px;font-size:.9rem;color:#cbd6e8}

          vertical-align:-1px;margin-right:5px}
</style>

<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>Knee Explorer</h1>
  <p class="lead">
    Sort the attention weights from largest to smallest and add them up. The

*A guided tour of retention knees, the narrowing domain factor, and why a
rising ratio is not evidence of convergence.*

---

## 1. The question, in one picture

You are reading something long. You cannot keep all of it. So you keep a few
things — the names, the key clause, the variable everything depends on — and let
the rest fade.

Machines that read text face the same problem in a form sharp enough to measure.
When a language model produces its next token it spreads attention across
everything it has read; most of the attention lands on very few places. So:
**how few places can you keep before the answer changes?**

Sort the positions from most-attended to least-attended and add up the weights.
The **retention curve** $M(k)$ is the mass held by the top $k$ positions. Fix a
tolerance $\tau$ — say you insist on preserving $98\%$ of the mass. The
**knee** is the smallest budget clearing the bar:

$$k^{*}(\tau) \;=\; \min\{\, k : M(k) \ge \tau \,\}.$$

That number is the honest price of memory. Everything below is about how it
behaves.

Play with the explorer before reading on. Drag the two peakedness sliders and
the bar; watch the knees move.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **What you should notice.** When the code curve sits above the prose curve at
> *every* budget, the code knee is below the prose knee at *every* bar — not just
> at the one you chose. That is not a coincidence; it is a theorem, and it is the
> right definition of "protected".

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: protection at every bar <em>is</em> dominance of curves</b></summary>

**Theorem.** Let $M_c$ and $M_q$ be retention curves, with $c$ a nonnegative
profile. Then
$$M_q(k) \le M_c(k) \ \text{ for every budget } k$$
if and only if, for every bar $\tau$ that prose can reach, code can reach it too
and $k^{*}_c(\tau) \le k^{*}_q(\tau)$.

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) The knee clears its own bar, so
$\tau \le M_q(k^{*}_q(\tau)) \le M_c(k^{*}_q(\tau))$, and the minimality of the
knee gives $k^{*}_c(\tau) \le k^{*}_q(\tau)$.

($\Leftarrow$) Fix a budget $k$ and apply the hypothesis at the *particular* bar
$\tau = M_q(k)$, which prose reaches at budget $k$. Then
$k^{*}_c(M_q(k)) \le k^{*}_q(M_q(k)) \le k$. Since the code knee clears its bar
and $M_c$ is nondecreasing,
$$M_q(k) \;\le\; M_c\bigl(k^{*}_c(M_q(k))\bigr) \;\le\; M_c(k). \qquad\blacksquare$$

The moral: a domain ordering that survives every threshold is a statement about
whole curves, so you never have to worry that "code is cheaper" was an artefact
of where the bar was set.
</details>

## 2. The measurement

Sweep the knee for **source code** and for **prose** at several context lengths:

| context | code knee | prose knee |
|---:|---:|---:|
| $512$ | $12$ | $16$ |
| $1024$ | $16$ | *(not yet measured)* |
| $4096$ | $32$ | $40$ |

Two things jump out.

**An acceleration.** Code goes $12 \to 16$ over the first doubling: four extra
keys. At that pace, two more doublings would land at $24$. The measurement says
$32$.

**A persistent but eroding discount.** Code is always cheaper: the ratio is
$12/16 = 0.75$ at short context and $32/40 = 0.80$ at long context. Code is
protected — but the protection appears to be wearing off, and the obvious
extrapolation is eventual parity.

That extrapolation is exactly wrong, and the rest of this page is about why.

---

## 3. First, a caveat that is a theorem

The code knee at $4096$ was found on a coarse grid: a budget of $28$ retained
about $0.976$ (fail) and $32$ retained $0.986$ (pass). Reported: $k^{*} = 32$.

But a fail at $28$ and a pass at $32$ prove only that the knee lies in
$\{29, 30, 31, 32\}$. And that bracket is *not improvable*.

> **Grid Ambiguity Theorem.** There are two nonnegative decreasing profiles that
> retain **exactly the same mass** at every budget at or below $28$ and at every
> budget at or above $32$, whose knees are $29$ and $32$ respectively.

Both candidate worlds are observationally identical outside the gap. The
reported $32$ is the top of a four-wide bracket, and only measurement inside the
gap can shrink it. Slide "grid spacing" in the explorer above down to $1$ and
watch the bracket collapse.

## 4. The model: one clock, two rates

The acceleration is a hint that context length is not the natural independent
variable. Something is undergoing a transition, and each domain rides the *same*
transition at its own rate. So introduce a shared coordinate $T$ —
"phase-transition time" — and posit that each domain's knee is affine in it:

$$K_d(T) \;=\; a_d + b_d\,T,$$

with $a_d$ the structural baseline of the domain and $b_d$ how hard the
transition inflates that domain's budget.

Now watch **two** observables, not one:

$$r(T) = \frac{K_{\text{code}}(T)}{K_{\text{prose}}(T)}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
G(T) = K_{\text{prose}}(T) - K_{\text{code}}(T).$$

This is the heart of the matter. The laboratory below lets you set all four
constants and watch both observables at once. **Start with the "Measured fit"
preset, then press "Parity rival" and look only at the ratio panel.**

{{interactive_demo:0}}

> **The trap, in one click.** The two presets produce *identical* ratios at the
> two measured contexts — $3/4$ and $4/5$ — but their ceilings are $5/6$ and $1$.
> One is permanent protection; the other is eventual parity. Nothing about the
> ratio's history distinguishes them. The gap panel separates them instantly:
> $4 \to 8$ versus $4 \to 4$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: narrowing is a sign condition, not a trend</b></summary>

**Theorem.** With $a_p > 0$, $b_p \ge 0$ and $0 \le T_1 < T_2$, the ratio
increases, $r(T_1) < r(T_2)$, **iff** $a_c b_p < a_p b_c$.

*Proof.* Both denominators are positive, so cross-multiplying,
$$r(T_1) < r(T_2)
\iff (a_c + b_c T_1)(a_p + b_p T_2) < (a_c + b_c T_2)(a_p + b_p T_1).$$
Expand: the $a_c a_p$ terms cancel, the $b_c b_p T_1 T_2$ terms cancel, and what
remains is
$$a_c b_p (T_2 - T_1) < a_p b_c (T_2 - T_1).$$
Since $T_2 - T_1 > 0$, this is equivalent to $a_c b_p < a_p b_c$. $\blacksquare$

So narrowing is not a trend that might continue or reverse — it is one fixed
inequality among four constants. It holds at all scales or none.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the ratio never reaches its own ceiling</b></summary>

**Theorem (exact error term).** If $b_p > 0$ and $K_p(T) > 0$ then
$$r(T) - \frac{b_c}{b_p} \;=\; \frac{a_c b_p - a_p b_c}{b_p\,K_p(T)} .$$

*Proof.* Put both terms over the common denominator $b_p(a_p + b_p T)$. The
numerator is $b_p(a_c + b_c T) - b_c(a_p + b_p T)$; the $T$-terms cancel
identically, leaving the constant $a_c b_p - a_p b_c$. $\blacksquare$

Two consequences. Under narrowing the numerator is negative, so
$r(T) < b_c/b_p$ for **every** $T$ — the ratio climbs strictly toward a ceiling
it never touches. And since $K_p(T) \to \infty$, the error decays like
$1/K_p(T)$, so $r(T) \to b_c/b_p$. Whether that ceiling is parity depends only on
$b_c$ versus $b_p$, which the ratio's history cannot see. The fourth panel in the
laboratory plots exactly this error on a log scale.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the permanence theorem</b></summary>

The gap is affine, $G(T) = (a_p - a_c) + (b_p - b_c)T$, so a growing gap forces
$b_c < b_p$ directly. Combining:

**Theorem (permanent protection).** Let $a_p, b_p > 0$ and $0 \le T_1 < T_2$.
If between two contexts *both* the ratio increased and the gap increased, then
$b_c < b_p$, hence
$$r(T) \;<\; \frac{b_c}{b_p} \;<\; 1 \qquad \text{for every } T \ge 0 .$$

The measured cell has ratios $3/4 \to 4/5$ and gaps $4 \to 8$. Both increased.
So the discount is permanent, and its floor is $b_c/b_p = 20/24 = 5/6$: **code
stays cheaper by a sixth, forever.**
</details>

## 5. The fit, and a prediction with something to lose

The measured numbers fit an affine pair exactly, with $T = 0$ at context $512$
and $T = 1$ at context $4096$:

$$K_{\text{code}}(T) = 12 + 20T, \qquad K_{\text{prose}}(T) = 16 + 24T .$$

All four measured knees, both ratios, both gaps, no residual. And there is a
bonus: the code knee $16$ at context $1024$ pins that context to $T = 1/5$, and
then the same fit *forces* the prose knee there to be

$$K_{\text{prose}}(1024) \;=\; 16 + \tfrac{24}{5} \;=\; \tfrac{104}{5} \;=\; 20.8 .$$

Nothing was fitted to produce that. A prose sweep landing on $20$ or $21$
corroborates the model; a landing at $24$ or above destroys it.

There is an even cheaper falsifier, requiring no fitting at all. For an affine
law take any three contexts and form the **normalised increment**

$$\rho \;=\; \frac{K(T_2) - K(T_1)}{K(T_3) - K(T_1)} \;=\; \frac{T_2 - T_1}{T_3 - T_1}.$$

The baseline cancels by subtraction and the slope by division: **$\rho$ does not
depend on the domain at all.** It is the knee analogue of a
[cross-ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-ratio), invariant under affine
reparametrisation — and the converse holds, so "one shared transition,
per-domain slopes" is *exactly* "equal normalised increments".

For the code chain $\rho = (16-12)/(32-12) = 1/5$, giving every domain on the
same transition the one-line forecast

$$K(4096) \;=\; K(512) + 5\,\bigl(K(1024) - K(512)\bigr).$$

A domain kneeing at $10, 14$ must knee at $30$; one at $14, 20$ at $44$; one at
$16, 24$ at $56$. Any single sweep that misses its line kills the model.

## 6. The acceleration is a broken concavity

What does "the acceleration hits code" mean, precisely? Index contexts by
doublings from $512$. A law of **diminishing returns** is one whose per-doubling
increments never grow.

> **Concave Chain Bound.** If $K(j+2) - K(j+1) \le K(j+1) - K(j)$ for all $j$,
> then $K(j) \le K(0) + j\,(K(1) - K(0))$.

Two-line induction: every increment is at most the first one, so $j$ steps add at
most $j$ times the first increment. Now apply it with $K(0) = 12$, $K(1) = 16$:
the cap at four doublings is $12 + 3\cdot 4 = 24$. The measurement is $32$.

**Every diminishing-returns law is refuted, by $8$ keys.** Not one curve — the
whole class.

{{visualization:1}}

<details>

Here is a genuine puzzle. The affine two-slope fit has *constant* increments in
$T$; it is not convex. Yet it reproduces a chain that refutes concavity. How?

The acceleration lives in the **clock**. The fit forces
$$T(0) = 0, \qquad T(1) = \tfrac15, \qquad T(3) = 1,$$
so the coordinate advances by $1/5$ over the first doubling and by $2/5$ per
doubling thereafter — with strictly increasing increments. Phase-transition time
races ahead of calendar time.

The domain responds linearly. **The transition accelerates.** That is a much more
interesting statement than "code got expensive faster than expected", and it is
what makes the shared-coordinate model testable across domains at all.

{{algorithm:2}}

## 7. Reading the verdict on attention itself

Everything so far has been about budgets. Push down to the attention weights and
something clean appears. Model the attention tail as exponential with decay rate
$\lambda$; keeping enough positions that the discarded tail falls below $\delta$
requires exactly

$$K(\lambda, \delta) \;=\; \frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\lambda}.$$

Two domains at the same tolerance therefore satisfy

$$\frac{K_{\text{code}}}{K_{\text{prose}}} \;=\; \frac{\lambda_{\text{prose}}}{\lambda_{\text{code}}} .$$

The domain factor is an **inverse ratio of decay rates**. "Code is protected"
says precisely: *code's attention is more sharply peaked than prose's.* And the
narrowing says the peakedness advantage is eroding — from $4/3$ at short context
to $5/4$ at $4096$, with a permanent floor of $6/5$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the chain pins the rates, and no harmonic law fits</b></summary>

From $K = 12, 16, 32$ at doublings $j = 0, 1, 3$, each knee gives
$\log(1/\delta) = K_j \lambda_j$, so
$$4\lambda_1 = 3\lambda_0, \qquad 8\lambda_3 = 3\lambda_0,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad \lambda_3 = \tfrac38\lambda_0 < \tfrac12\lambda_0 .$$
An affine knee law would put the long-context rate at $\lambda_0/2$; the
measurement forces it strictly below. The degradation is **super-harmonic**.

Worse for the simple story: the natural family of rate laws — the one equivalent
to "each doubling costs a fixed number of extra keys" — is the generalised
harmonic family $\lambda_j = C/(j+c)$. Writing $L = \log(1/\delta)$, each knee
becomes $L(j + c) = K_j C$, so
$$Lc = 12C, \qquad L(1+c) = 16C, \qquad L(3+c) = 32C .$$
Subtracting consecutively gives $L = 4C$ and $2L = 16C$, i.e. $L = 8C$. Hence
$C = 0$, which is impossible. **No member of the family fits, for any $C$ and any
offset.** The acceleration is a change of *shape*, not of scale.
</details>

---

## 8. Is it just the tokenizer?

The obvious objection: perhaps code only looks cheaper because tokenizers chop
code and prose at different granularity. Suppose each code unit becomes $r_c$
tokens and each prose unit $r_p$. Then protection survives whenever

$$r_c \cdot K_{\text{code}} \;\le\; r_p \cdot (K_{\text{prose}} - 1),$$

and in particular whenever the tokenizer is **no coarser on code than on prose**,
$r_c \le r_p$ — which covers every realistic case. The condition is not
decorative: with $r_c = 8$, $r_p = 1$ the diluted code knee provably exceeds the
diluted prose knee. So protection is a genuine, and mild, constraint.

There is also a companion negative result worth stating. A *purely
multiplicative* domain model — code's knee a fixed constant times prose's, which
is what a pure tokenisation mechanism predicts — is refuted by **any** change in
the ratio. The ratio demonstrably moved from $3/4$ to $4/5$. Therefore an
**additive** structural term is required: the $a_d$ in the law is real, and the
data insists on it.
